notes.definition: DNA is the chemical that makes up the genetic material in the nucleus. It is a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix, and it is found in chromosomes. A gene is a small section of DNA that codes for a particular protein, and the genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.
explanation: The genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is made of a chemical called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). DNA is a polymer: a very large molecule made of many repeating units joined together. A DNA molecule consists of two strands that are twisted around each other to form a shape called a double helix, a bit like a twisted ladder.

DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes. Each chromosome is one very long DNA molecule that is tightly coiled so that it fits inside the nucleus. In human body cells there are 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each chromosome carries many genes.

Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids. When the amino acids are joined in that sequence, they make a specific protein. Proteins include enzymes, some hormones, antibodies and structural proteins such as collagen. Because the proteins a cell makes control its structure and activities, genes control the characteristics of an organism.

The genome of an organism is the entire genetic material of that organism: all of the DNA in one set of its chromosomes. The whole human genome has now been studied (the Human Genome Project was completed in 2003), and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.

Understanding the human genome is important for three main reasons. Scientists can search for genes linked to different types of disease, such as some cancers, so people at risk can be screened and monitored. It helps in the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders such as cystic fibrosis, for example by developing new drugs or gene therapy. It can also be used to trace human migration patterns from the past, because comparing small differences in the DNA of people from different parts of the world shows how populations are related and how they spread.
keyFacts: The genetic material in the nucleus is made of DNA.
DNA is a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix.
DNA is contained in structures called chromosomes.
A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome.
Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein.
The genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.
The whole human genome has now been studied.
Uses of the human genome: finding genes linked to disease, understanding and treating inherited disorders, tracing past human migration.

keyTerms.definition: Deoxyribonucleic acid: a polymer made of two strands forming a double helix, which makes up the genetic material.

The shape of a DNA molecule: two strands twisted around each other.
A structure in the nucleus made of one long, coiled DNA molecule carrying many genes.

workedExamples.title: Ordering genetic structures
workedExamples.question: Put these in order of size, starting with the largest: gene, genome, chromosome, nucleus.
steps: The nucleus contains all the chromosomes, so it is the largest structure here. (The genome is the total genetic material, which is stored in the nucleus.)
Each chromosome is one DNA molecule carrying many genes.
A gene is only a small section of one chromosome.

workedExamples.title: From gene to characteristic
workedExamples.question: Explain how a gene can control a characteristic such as eye colour.
steps: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids.
The amino acids are joined in that order to make a specific protein.
The protein (for example an enzyme that makes a pigment) affects the characteristic, such as the amount of pigment in the iris.
workedExamples.answer: The gene codes for the sequence of amino acids in a protein; the protein produced affects the characteristic.

workedExamples.title: Using genome data
workedExamples.question: In a study, 360 out of 1200 people with a type of heart disease had the same variant of a gene, compared with 60 out of 1200 people without the disease. Calculate the percentage in each group and suggest what this shows.
steps: The variant is six times more common in people with the disease, so the gene may be linked to the disease. This is a correlation and other factors may be involved.
workedExamples.answer: 30% and 5%; the gene variant is linked to (correlated with) the disease.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a gene and a chromosome are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact a chromosome is a whole DNA molecule carrying many genes; a gene is only a small section of it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the genome is one gene or one chromosome.
misconceptions.right: In fact the genome is the entire genetic material of an organism.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think genes are made of protein.
misconceptions.right: In fact genes are made of DNA. Genes code for proteins, which are made from amino acids.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that knowing the human genome means all diseases can now be cured.
misconceptions.right: In fact studying the genome helps scientists find genes linked to diseases and develop treatments, but most diseases are not yet curable and many are affected by several genes and the environment.

realWorld: Women can be tested for faulty versions of the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, which greatly increase the risk of breast cancer, so they can choose extra screening or preventive surgery.
Comparing the DNA of people around the world has shown that modern humans originated in Africa and migrated to other continents.
Knowing the exact gene that causes cystic fibrosis has allowed scientists to develop new drugs that target the faulty protein, and to research gene therapy.
examTips: Learn the definition of a gene word for word: 'a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein'.
When asked for the importance of the human genome, give the three spec uses: genes linked to disease, inherited disorders, and human migration patterns.
Do not confuse 'genome' (all genetic material) with 'gene' (one section of DNA).
If asked to describe the structure of DNA in this topic, use the key words 'polymer', 'two strands' and 'double helix'.

questions.question: What is the genetic material in the nucleus made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: DNA
questions.explanation: Genetic material is DNA. Proteins are made from amino acids, and genes code for proteins.

markScheme: 1 mark: a double helix

questions.question: What is a gene?
options: A small section of DNA on a chromosome
All the DNA in an organism
markScheme: 1 mark: a small section of DNA on a chromosome
questions.explanation: A gene is a small section of DNA. All the DNA of an organism is its genome, and genes code for proteins rather than being proteins.

questions.question: What is the genome of an organism?
options: The entire genetic material of the organism
markScheme: 1 mark: the entire genetic material of the organism
questions.explanation: The genome is all of an organism's genetic material, not one gene or one chromosome.

questions.question: DNA is a polymer. What does this mean?
options: It is found only in the nucleus
It is made of many repeating units joined together
markScheme: 1 mark: it is made of many repeating units joined together
questions.explanation: A polymer is a large molecule built from many smaller repeating units. DNA is also found in bacteria, which have no nucleus, and it has two strands.

questions.question: What does each gene code for?
options: A particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein
markScheme: 1 mark: a particular sequence of amino acids to make a specific protein
questions.explanation: Genes carry the code for the order of amino acids in a protein.

questions.question: Which list is in order of size, from largest to smallest?
markScheme: 1 mark: nucleus, chromosome, gene
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains chromosomes, and each chromosome carries many genes.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a reason given for the importance of understanding the human genome?
options: Searching for genes linked to different types of disease
Changing the genes of every person at birth
Tracing human migration patterns from the past
Understanding and treatment of inherited disorders
markScheme: 1 mark: changing the genes of every person at birth
questions.explanation: The three uses in the specification are disease genes, inherited disorders and migration patterns. Changing everyone's genes is not a use and would raise serious ethical issues.

questions.question: Scientists compared DNA from people living in different parts of the world. People from populations that separated longer ago had more differences in their DNA. How does this help scientists?
options: It allows them to trace human migration patterns from the past
It shows which people have inherited disorders
It proves that all humans have identical genomes
It shows that DNA changes into protein
markScheme: 1 mark: it allows them to trace human migration patterns from the past
questions.explanation: Differences in DNA build up over time, so the number of differences between populations indicates how long ago they separated. This is used to work out how humans migrated.

questions.question:
Scientists investigated whether a gene variant is linked to a disease.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which is the best conclusion from the results in Table 1?
options: The variant definitely causes the disease
The variant is strongly linked to the disease
There is little evidence that the variant is linked to the disease
Everyone with the variant will get the disease
markScheme: 1 mark: there is little evidence that the variant is linked to the disease
questions.explanation: The percentages are almost the same in both groups, so the variant does not appear to be linked to the disease. Even a large difference would show a correlation, not proof of cause.

markScheme: 1 mark: the gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids
1 mark: which makes a specific protein (that produces or affects the characteristic)
questions.explanation: Genes work by coding for proteins. The protein made, for example an enzyme or a structural protein, determines the characteristic.

questions.question: Give three reasons why understanding the human genome is important for the future.
markScheme: 1 mark: search for genes linked to different types of disease
1 mark: understanding and treatment of inherited disorders
1 mark: tracing human migration patterns from the past
questions.explanation: These are the three applications given in the specification.

questions.question: Explain how finding a gene linked to a type of cancer could benefit people.
markScheme: 1 mark: people can be tested to see if they have the gene / know their risk
1 mark: so they can have more frequent checks for early detection / make lifestyle changes / preventive treatment / scientists can develop targeted drugs
questions.explanation: Knowing which gene variants increase disease risk allows screening and earlier treatment, which improves survival.

questions.question:
A student said:
'Each chromosome is a gene.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: a chromosome is one long molecule of DNA
1 mark: that carries many genes; a gene is only a small section of the DNA
questions.explanation: The relationship is one chromosome to many genes. Each gene is a short length of the chromosome's DNA.

questions.question: Suggest why studying the genome of an individual patient could help doctors choose the best drug to treat them.
acceptedAnswers: genes affect how body responds to drugs
markScheme: 1 mark: people have different variants of genes
1 mark: which code for different proteins (for example enzymes that break down drugs)
1 mark: so a drug can be chosen that will be most effective / cause fewer side effects for that person
questions.explanation: This is an application of genome knowledge: the proteins coded for by a patient's genes affect how drugs work in their body, so treatment can be matched to the genome.

questions.question:
Human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.
How many chromosomes are in a human body cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 46
questions.explanation: 23 pairs × 2 = 46 chromosomes.

questions.question:
Scientists studied a gene variant in two groups of people.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate how many more people with the disease had the variant than people without the disease.
questions.explanation: Convert each percentage to a number: 28% of 2500 = 700 and 8% of 2500 = 200, so the difference is 500. Subtracting percentages (20%) and then finding 20% of 2500 also gives 500 because the groups are the same size.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between the nucleus, chromosomes, DNA, genes and proteins.
markScheme: Indicative content: genetic material in the nucleus; made of DNA; DNA is a polymer of two strands in a double helix; DNA is contained in chromosomes; each chromosome is one long DNA molecule; a gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome; each chromosome carries many genes; each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids; which makes a specific protein; the genome is all of the genetic material.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear, logical description linking all or most of the terms in the correct hierarchy, including that genes code for amino acid sequences to make proteins.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct statements about two or three of the terms with limited linking.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Work from the largest structure down: nucleus contains chromosomes, chromosomes are DNA, genes are sections of DNA, genes code for proteins.

questions.question: The whole human genome has now been studied. Discuss the importance of understanding the human genome. In your answer give examples and consider any limitations or concerns.
markScheme: Indicative content. Uses: search for genes linked to different types of disease (for example genes increasing the risk of some cancers); people can be tested and screened, have earlier checks or make lifestyle changes; understanding and treatment of inherited disorders (for example cystic fibrosis), new drugs, gene therapy, embryo screening; tracing human migration patterns by comparing DNA of populations (for example humans spreading out of Africa); possible personalised medicine. Limitations or concerns: most diseases are influenced by many genes and the environment, so having a gene variant does not mean a person will get a disease; knowing about a risk may cause anxiety; genetic information could be misused, for example by insurers or employers; privacy of genetic data; treatments are not yet available for many disorders.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed discussion of all three spec uses with examples, plus at least one well explained limitation or concern.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes at least two uses with some explanation, may mention a limitation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of one or two uses.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Discuss means give the importance with examples and balance it with limitations. Linking each use to a concrete example (for example cystic fibrosis or human migration from Africa) moves an answer to the top level.
